title: The Two Players: Inner Integral vs. Twice the Speed
content: The reduction rests on naming two functions of the curve parameter `t`. `innerIntegral γ t` is the inner angular integral `∫ θ in 0..π, |γ'ₓ(t)·sin θ + γ'ᵧ(t)·cos θ|` — *definitionally* the integrand that appears inside the parent file's `hInnerInt` hypothesis. `twiceSpeed γ t` is `2·√(γ'ₓ(t)² + γ'ᵧ(t)²) = 2‖γ'(t)‖`, twice the Euclidean speed of the curve. Both are `noncomputable` because they involve `Real.sqrt` and a Bochner integral. The entire file amounts to the single claim that these two functions coincide (`innerIntegral γ = twiceSpeed γ`); once that equality is in hand, every analytic property of the intimidating parametrized integral is read off from the elementary speed function instead.

title: The Inner Integral is Twice the Speed
content: `innerIntegral_eq` proves that the inner angular integral, viewed as a function of the curve parameter `t`, is *equal everywhere* to `2‖γ'(t)‖`. The proof is `funext t` followed by a single application of the parent file's `angular_average (deriv (Prod.fst ∘ γ) t) (deriv (Prod.snd ∘ γ) t)`. Crucially, `angular_average` holds for *every* pair `(a, b)` with no hypotheses, so the resulting equality of functions is unconditional — it needs nothing about γ. This is the whole engine of the reduction: the integrability question about a scary-looking parametrized integral collapses to an integrability question about `2√(x'² + y'²)`.
mathContext: $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi |\gamma_x'(t)\sin\theta + \gamma_y'(t)\cos\theta|\,d\theta = 2\sqrt{\gamma_x'(t)^2 + \gamma_y'(t)^2} = 2\lVert\gamma'(t)\rVert$ for every $t$, by the angular-average identity applied pointwise.

title: Continuity Transfers Through the Square Root
content: Once `innerIntegral γ = twiceSpeed γ` is available, continuity of the inner-integral function follows from continuity of the component derivatives. `innerIntegral_continuousOn` rewrites with `innerIntegral_eq`, unfolds `twiceSpeed`, and builds continuity compositionally: `continuousOn_const.mul (((hx.pow 2).add (hy.pow 2)).sqrt)`. The `.sqrt` combinator (`ContinuousOn.sqrt`) is what closes the gap — `Real.sqrt` is continuous everywhere (including at 0), so no positivity side-condition on the speed is needed. A global-continuity twin `innerIntegral_continuous` uses the analogous `Continuous.*` lemmas.
mathContext: If $\gamma_x', \gamma_y'$ are continuous then $t \mapsto 2\sqrt{\gamma_x'(t)^2 + \gamma_y'(t)^2}$ is continuous, since polynomials and $\sqrt{\cdot}$ are continuous and composition preserves continuity.

title: Discharging hInnerInt: Continuity ⟹ Interval-Integrability
content: `hInnerInt_of_continuousOn` produces exactly the hypothesis the parent theorems demand — `IntervalIntegrable (fun t => ∫ θ in 0..π, |…|) volume a b` — from continuity of the derivatives on `uIcc a b`. The proof is a one-liner: `(innerIntegral_continuousOn γ hx hy).intervalIntegrable`. The bridge `ContinuousOn.intervalIntegrable` turns continuity on the interval into interval-integrability with no measure-theoretic estimate. Because `innerIntegral γ` is *definitionally* the parametrized integral, the result unifies with the parent's statement directly. This is the sentence that answers the open question: the integrability hypothesis was never independent.
mathContext: A function continuous on a compact interval $[a,b]$ is (Riemann/Lebesgue) integrable there. Formally: $\text{ContinuousOn } f\, [a,b] \Rightarrow \text{IntervalIntegrable } f\, \mu\, a\, b$.

title: Removing hInnerInt from the Statement
content: `buffon_smooth_of_continuousOn` and its global-continuity twin `buffon_smooth_of_continuous` strip `hInnerInt` out of the parent's `buffon_smooth_full` by supplying it internally through `hInnerInt_of_continuousOn`/`hInnerInt_of_continuous`. What survives in the signature is only honest analytic data: pointwise differentiability (`HasDerivAt` for both coordinate functions on `uIcc a b`) plus continuity of the derivatives. The conclusion is the exact Buffon–Barbier identity `concreteSmoothExpectedCrossings γ a b d = 2·planarArcLength γ a b/(π·d)`. These are the intermediate forms of the theorem; the final section collapses both the differentiability and the continuity requirements into the single, natural hypothesis `ContDiff ℝ 1`.
mathContext: $\text{concreteSmoothExpectedCrossings}\,\gamma\,a\,b\,d = \dfrac{2\,\text{planarArcLength}\,\gamma\,a\,b}{\pi d},$ assuming only that each coordinate is differentiable with a continuous derivative on $[a,b]$ — the integrability side-condition is discharged internally rather than assumed.

title: C¹ is Exactly the Right Hypothesis
content: `buffon_smooth_of_contDiff` is the payoff: for any curve whose coordinate functions are `ContDiff ℝ 1`, the Buffon–Barbier formula E[crossings] = 2L/(πd) holds with *no* integrability, Fubini, or differentiability conditions in the signature. C¹ supplies both missing ingredients at once — `ContDiff.differentiable le_rfl` gives `HasDerivAt (…) (deriv (…) t) t` at every point (feeding the parent's `hdx`/`hdy`), and `ContDiff.continuous_deriv le_rfl` gives continuity of the derivative (feeding `hInnerInt_of_continuous`). This is the natural analytic hypothesis of the classical 1860 theorem, now stated cleanly in Lean.
mathContext: For a $C^1$ planar curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^2$ with arc length $L$, the expected number of crossings of a random line grid of spacing $d$ is $\mathbb{E}[\text{crossings}] = \dfrac{2L}{\pi d}$ (Barbier, 1860).
